content: The availability of essential drugs and blood, as well as basic emergency obstetric care, must be ensured 24 hours a day at both hospitals and clinics. Improvements in emergency obstetric care are directly relevant to efforts aimed at enhancing trauma care through quality improvement (QI) programs. In both scenarios, it is critical to establish systems for emergency transport from the field. Healthcare facilities must also have the capacity for resuscitation, including access to blood, and the ability to perform basic surgical procedures. This requires both human resources (skills and staffing) and physical resources (equipment and supplies) to ensure these procedures are carried out safely. The examples from obstetric care highlight the significant benefits that can result from better organization and planning of services through QI programs. Furthermore, improving the quality of medical care via QI programs has been shown by the Disease Control Priorities Project (DCPP) to be highly cost-effective. Cost-effectiveness ratios for such initiatives range from $4 to $28 per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted in settings with high disease prevalence and poor existing care quality. Additionally, QI programs themselves can lead to cost savings. A DALY is a measure of the public health burden of diseases, accounting for years of life lost by subtracting the age at death from life expectancy. It also includes the burden from non-fatal conditions by considering the percentage loss in function. For instance, a condition that leaves someone at 50% functional capacity results in half the DALY losses of a fatal condition. The total burden of disease is calculated by summing losses from both fatal and non-fatal outcomes. Similarly, the public health impact of interventions can be assessed by estimating the number of DALY losses they avert. Quality improvement (QI) programs are widely recognized as a cornerstone of trauma systems in high-income countries. For example, in the United Kingdom, the British Trauma Society mandates that all hospitals treating major trauma patients must have an audit program to maintain quality standards in trauma care. In the United States, the American College of Surgeons (ACS) has established criteria for hospitals to meet in order to be designated as trauma centers. These criteria are detailed in the publication Resources for Optimal Care of the Injured Patient. The presence and proper functioning of a QI program is a critical factor in trauma center verification visits by the ACS, and deficiencies in QI programs are the most common reason for unsuccessful reviews. A review of 179 hospital verification visits revealed that the leading cause of unsuccessful reviews was the absence or inadequacy of QI programs. Common deficiencies included failure to address identified problems, lack of documentation (e.g., physician response times), non-adherence to protocols, lack of attendance at regular multidisciplinary QI conferences, and underutilization of trauma registries to support QI efforts. The authors of this review emphasized the need for greater understanding and emphasis on QI programs when developing trauma systems. Even in high-income countries, there is considerable room for improvement in trauma QI programs. For example, a survey of 161 hospitals in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland found varying levels of compliance with trauma care standards. The situation is even more pronounced in lowand middle-income countries. A study conducted as part of the Essential Trauma Care Project assessed trauma care capabilities at 100 healthcare facilities in Ghana, India, Mexico, and Vietnam. This study found a complete absence of formal trauma-related QI programs and trauma registries with severity adjustment. Given the global lack of trauma QI activities and the low cost and potential benefits of such initiatives, it is strongly recommended to enhance trauma QI efforts worldwide. This can be achieved through formal QI programs in larger hospitals or by integrating trauma cases into broader QI programs in smaller facilities. Efforts to promote greater implementation of trauma QI globally should build on existing foundations, such as morbidity and mortality (M&M) conferences, which are already conducted in many hospitals. M&M conferences involve discussions of deaths and complications to identify preventable factors. These conferences are widely held in hospitals with formal medical specialty departments and often include trauma cases, especially in hospitals with surgical departments. The peer review process in M&M conferences serves as the foundation for improvements in medical care through more formal QI programs. To optimize their effectiveness, M&M conferences should not only discuss deaths and complications but also identify problems and take corrective actions to address them. M&M conferences should be held regularly, with their frequency determined by the institution's trauma volume. Hospitals with higher trauma volumes may hold trauma-specific M&M conferences weekly, while those with lower volumes may address trauma-related deaths and complications on a monthly basis. These conferences should be viewed as opportunities to identify and correct problems, with a focus on systems issues, developing corrective action plans, implementing these plans, and evaluating their outcomes. A separate multidisciplinary trauma QI committee can extend the work of M&M conferences. In larger hospitals, this committee may function as a standalone entity, led by a designated trauma director with adequate administrative support. This support includes a trauma program manager and administrative assistants responsible for logistics, data processing, resource allocation, and communication with the various teams involved in trauma care. Active participation from the entire trauma and critical care teams, as well as other specialties such as anesthesia, orthopedics, emergency medicine, neurosurgery, transfusion services, and radiology, is essential for the success of the QI process. In conclusion, while M&M conferences and trauma QI programs are already in place in many hospitals, their potential to improve trauma care globally is not fully realized. Greater attention to procedural details, problem identification, corrective action planning, and follow-through is needed to maximize their impact.
